headline: Sea Girt Reef, 65 Feet: Sea Bass to 4 Pounds While the Mud Hole Waits on Bluefin
subhead: Canyon tuna keep building at Hudson, Wilmington and Washington, but the inshore lumps haven't turned on yet — here's where the book paid off this week.
body_markdown:
Sea Girt Reef, 65 feet, four miles off the inlet — that number has been in my book since 2007 and it hasn't stopped paying rent. This week the tugboat wrecks on the north end of the reef held sea bass stacked two and three deep on the fish finder, and we boated fish to 4 pounds on double-hook rigs tipped with clam and squid strips, bounced tight to the structure on the last two hours of the incoming. That's the pattern right now up and down this stretch — Axel Carlson Reef running the same depth range is doing the same thing, and Shrewsbury Rocks in the shallower 40 to 50 foot water is holding smaller fish but plenty of them. The sea bass bite has been the one thing I could set a watch by all summer, and August hasn't changed that. Bring 6-ounce bank sinkers if you're fishing the reef on a moving tide — current's been stout enough to require it, especially around the new moon push.

Now here's the honest part of the report. The Mud Hole lumps — the ones I mark bluefin on most Augusts once the bait piles up over that broken bottom in 60 to 90 feet — haven't shown me a thing yet this week. I ran out three times looking for the diving birds and the nervous water that usually tips off a bluefin push onto the structure, and what I found instead was clean, quiet water and bait sitting deep, not balled up tight the way it needs to be for those fish to commit. The Klondike was the same story — good sea bass down deep on the rockpile stretches, but no sign of tuna working the lumps. I'm not going to sell you a bite that isn't there. If the bluefin are around, they're still holding out past the 20-fathom curve, which lines up with what the canyon boats have been marking.

And that's where the real story has been. Hudson, Wilmington and Washington canyons have had one of the better stretches of yellowfin trolling I've seen in a few Julys, and that pattern carried straight into this week. We called this three weeks back — said the stable high pressure was quietly building one of the better July tuna setups in recent memory, with yellowfin and some bigeye activity improving at those three canyons, all within range of a Manasquan run — and that's exactly the pattern that's held. Boats working spreads of green machines and cedar plugs off the temp breaks on the edges of those canyons are still connecting, with bluefin mixed in on the troll and some chunking success once the sun gets high and the fish go quiet on the surface baits. The tide range is narrowing into the coming neap around August 5-6, and when current softens like that, trolling tends to outproduce chunking — the bait doesn't stack as hard on structure, and a moving spread covers more water than a static chunk slick can. If you've got the range for a canyon run this week, that's where I'd put my gas money before I'd burn it hunting bluefin on the inshore lumps.

Mahi have started showing the way they always do this time of year — not on the reef structure, but out past Barnegat Ridge and the Klondike on the pot buoys and any bit of floating junk you can find drifting the warm filaments pushing in off the Gulf Stream edge. We picked up a mixed bag of schoolie mahi, a couple pushing 6 pounds, working small bucktails and strips of squid around lobster pot warps in maybe 25 to 30 fathoms east of the ridge. That's textbook August timing for this fishery — the pots concentrate bait, the mahi sit under them, and if you're patient enough to work every buoy you pass instead of running past them, you'll put a few in the box. Water out there was reading warm and clean, close to 76 degrees on the surface, with a moderate three-foot swell out of the southeast that made for a comfortable ride but did put a little push on the drift — light jig heads worked better than straight bucktails to keep baits down in the strike zone.

Bonito haven't shown yet on our reefs, and with the swell and warm surface water sitting the way it is, I wouldn't expect them for another week or two — that's more of a late-August, early-September pattern for us once the bait pods tighten up over structure like Sea Girt and Shrewsbury Rocks. Tog and cod are off the table this time of year in these depths, so I won't pretend otherwise.

Looking ahead, I'd keep sea bass trips locked into the reef and wreck network — that bite has been the most reliable thing on my numbers all season and nothing about the conditions suggests it's slowing. For tuna, I'd still favor the canyon run over the inshore lumps until I see bait ball up tight and birds working the Mud Hole again — if that changes with the softening tide this week, I'll be the first one out there checking it. Keep an eye on the pot lines past the ridge for mahi through the rest of August; that pattern usually holds as long as the warm water keeps pushing inshore.
